# Simple Regression *** Suppose we have some bivariate data: $\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i}$. In the previous chapter, we summarized the strength of association between two variables using correlation. Correlation tells us *how strongly* $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ move together, but not *by how much* $\hat{y}$ changes per unit change in $\hat{x}$. Regression answers that question by fitting a line through the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Pull two columns from USArrests and rename for compact code below xy_hat <- USArrests[, c('UrbanPop', 'Murder')] colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=urban population share, y_hat=murder arrests per 100K # Scatter the data plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, xy_hat, col=grey(0, .5), pch=16, main=NA, xlab='Population Share in Urban Area', ylab='Murder Arrests per 100K') title('Data from American States, 1975', font.main=1) # Pearson Correlation cor(xy_hat$x_hat, xy_hat$y_hat) ## [1] 0.06957262 # Fit the line via OLS and overlay it on the scatter reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat) abline(reg, lty=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: :::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"} A *fitted value* $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}$ is the model's prediction for observation $i$. The superscript $\mathrm{fit}$ marks a fitted value, while $\hat{y}_{i}$ is an observed outcome. The *sample residual* is the gap between actual and fitted, $\hat{e}_{i} = \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}$. *Ordinary least squares* (OLS) fits a model by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{e}_{i}^{2}$. ::: We square the residuals so that positive and negative errors do not cancel, and so that big misses are penalized more than small ones. ## Simple Linear Regression This refers to fitting a linear model to bivariate data. #### **Model and Objective** {-} A regression line goes through the cloud of points. To calculate it, we need some definitions first. :::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"} Our *simple linear model* is $$ \hat{y}_{i}=b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}+\hat{e}_{i}, $$ where $b_{0}$ and $b_{1}$ are the coefficients, and $\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i}$ are the data for observation $i$. ::: The residual $\hat{e}_{i}$ is the vertical gap between observation $i$'s actual value of $\hat{y}_{i}$ and the model's prediction for that observation: $$\hat{e}_{i}=\hat{y}_{i}-(b_{0}+b_{1}\hat{x}_{i}).$$ During minimization, $\hat{e}_{i}$ depends on the trial coefficients $b_{0}, b_{1}$; the final residuals use the fitted coefficients $\hat{b}_{0}, \hat{b}_{1}$. For the linear model, the OLS problem is $$\begin{aligned} \min_{b_{0}, b_{1}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{e}_{i} \right)^2 &= \min_{b_{0}, b_{1}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right)^2. \end{aligned}$$ We could find the best-fitting coefficients numerically, by trying out different combinations of $(b_{0}, b_{1})$. You can do that in this [example](https://myshiny.duckdns.org/least-squares/), which can help you understand what is happening. This problem has an analytic solution, however, which means we know that the optimal OLS slope and intercept are $$\hat{b}_{1} = \frac{\hat{c}_{XY}}{\hat{v}_{X}}, \qquad \hat{b}_{0} = \hat{m}_{Y} - \hat{b}_{1} \hat{m}_{X}.$$ The computer uses this math to find the coefficients quickly. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Run a Simple Regression reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat) coef(reg) ## (Intercept) x_hat ## 6.41594246 0.02093466 # Manual verification x_hat <- xy_hat[, 'x_hat'] y_hat <- xy_hat[, 'y_hat'] b1 <- cov( x_hat, y_hat)/var(x_hat) b1 ## [1] 0.02093466 b0 <- mean(y_hat) - b1*mean(x_hat) b0 ## [1] 6.415942 ``` ::: The *least-squares slope* $\hat{b}_{1}$ seeks to answer "how much does the prediction $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{fit}}$ change per one-unit change in $\hat{x}$?" When the data are not known to be linearly related, the formula shows the slope is generally just the covariance divided by the variance of $\hat{x}$. As such, $\hat{b}_{1}$ is generally interpreted as a summary statistic for associations, just like the correlation. In fact, $\hat{b}_{1} = \hat{r}_{XY} \cdot \hat{s}_{Y}/\hat{s}_{X}$, so the simple regression slope is a rescaled version of the Pearson correlation statistic. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coef(reg) ## (Intercept) x_hat ## 6.41594246 0.02093466 # Slope from correlation: R_{XY} * S_Y / S_X cor(xy_hat$x_hat, xy_hat$y_hat) * sd(xy_hat$y_hat)/sd(xy_hat$x_hat) ## [1] 0.02093466 ``` ::: The intercept guarantees the fitted line passes through the point of means $(\hat{m}_{X}, \hat{m}_{Y})$. To see why, add $\hat{b}_{1}\hat{m}_{X}$ to both sides of the intercept formula to get $\hat{m}_{Y} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1}\hat{m}_{X}$. This says that the line's height at $\hat{m}_{X}$ is exactly $\hat{m}_{Y}$. :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Derive the OLS intercept and slope by taking the partial derivative of the objective with respect to each coefficient and setting it to zero. Start with the intercept. By the chain rule, the derivative of each squared term with respect to $b_{0}$ is $-2$ times the residual: $$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \frac{\partial}{\partial b_{0}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right)^2 \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} -2\left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right). \end{aligned}$$ Divide both sides by $-2n$, and use the means $\hat{m}_{X} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{x}_{i}/n$ and $\hat{m}_{Y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{y}_{i}/n$: $$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{y}_{i} - b_{0} - b_{1} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{x}_{i} \\ &= \hat{m}_{Y} - b_{0} - b_{1} \hat{m}_{X} \\ \Rightarrow \hat{b}_{0} &= \hat{m}_{Y} - \hat{b}_{1}\hat{m}_{X}. \end{aligned}$$ Now the slope. The derivative of each squared term with respect to $b_{1}$ is $-2 \hat{x}_{i}$ times the residual: $$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \frac{\partial}{\partial b_{1}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right)^2 \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} -2\left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right) \hat{x}_{i}. \end{aligned}$$ Divide both sides by $-2$, substitute the intercept $b_{0} = \hat{m}_{Y} - b_{1}\hat{m}_{X}$, and split the sum in two: $$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( [\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}] - b_{1} [\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}] \right) \hat{x}_{i} \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) \hat{x}_{i} - b_{1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}) \hat{x}_{i}. \end{aligned}$$ Deviations from the mean sum to zero, so $\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) \hat{m}_{X} = 0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}) \hat{m}_{X} = 0$. Subtracting these from the two sums replaces each trailing $\hat{x}_{i}$ with $\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}$: $$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) - b_{1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})^2 \\ \Rightarrow \hat{b}_{1} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X})^2}. \end{aligned}$$ Dividing the top and bottom by $n$ gives $\hat{b}_{1} = \hat{c}_{XY}/\hat{v}_{X}$. This point is a minimum and not a maximum because each squared residual is U-shaped in the coefficients, so their sum is bowl-shaped in $(b_{0}, b_{1})$ and the only point where both derivatives are zero is the bottom of the bowl. ::: #### **Predictions** {-} Plugging the coefficients into the line gives the fitted value for observation $i$: $$\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1} \hat{x}_{i}.$$ Fitted values are useful for *in-sample* diagnostics: comparing $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}$ to $\hat{y}_{i}$ shows where the model fits well and where it misses (these are the residuals $\hat{e}_{i}$ we minimized). Predictions at new values are useful for *out-of-sample* questions like "what murder arrest rate would the model predict for a state with 70 percent of people in urban areas?". A *prediction* $$\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x) = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1} x$$ uses the same line at any design point $x$. A fitted value is the prediction at a sample point: $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(\hat{x}_{i})$. Making predictions far away from your observations is risky, with no nearby data to anchor its prediction. Also note that a model can predict well and still not tell us what would happen. For example, a store's daily umbrella sales predict its raincoat sales well, yet a discount that raises umbrella sales need not raise raincoat sales. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Find predicted values and residuals predict(reg) resid(reg) # Manual verification y_fit <- b0+b1*x_hat y_fit e_hat <- y_hat - y_fit e_hat ``` ::: :::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"} Suppose we have a dataset with $n = 3$ observations: $\{(1,2), (2,2.5), (3,4)\}$. We can compute the regression coefficients and model predictions in five steps. Step 1. Sample Means $$\begin{aligned} \hat{m}_{X} &= \frac{1+2+3}{3} = 2 \\ \hat{m}_{Y} &= \frac{2 + 2.5 + 4}{3} = \frac{17}{6}. \end{aligned}$$ Step 2. Covariance and Variance \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} i & \hat{x}_{i} & \hat{y}_{i} & (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}) & (\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) & (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) & (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})^2 \\ \hline 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 & -\tfrac{5}{6} & \tfrac{5}{6} & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2.5 & 0 & -\tfrac{1}{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 1 & \tfrac{7}{6} & \tfrac{7}{6} & 1 \\ \end{array} $$\begin{aligned} \hat{c}_{XY} &= \sum_{i=1}^3 (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) /3 = [\tfrac{5}{6} + \tfrac{7}{6}]/3 = 2/3 \\ \hat{v}_{X} &= \sum_{i=1}^3 (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})^2 / 3 = [1 + 1]/3 = 2/3. \end{aligned}$$ Step 3. Slope and Intercept $$ \hat{b}_{1} = \frac{\hat{c}_{XY}}{\hat{v}_{X}} = \frac{2/3}{2/3} = 1, $$ $$ \hat{b}_{0} = \hat{m}_{Y} - \hat{b}_{1} \hat{m}_{X} = \frac{17}{6} - 2 = \frac{5}{6} \approx 0.83. $$ $$ \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1} \hat{x}_{i} = \frac{5}{6} + \hat{x}_{i}. $$ Step 4. Fitted Values and Residuals $$ \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} i & \hat{x}_{i} & \hat{y}_{i} & \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \tfrac{5}{6} + \hat{x}_{i} & \hat{e}_{i} = \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} \\ \hline 1 & 1 & 2 & \tfrac{11}{6} & \tfrac{1}{6} \\ 2 & 2 & 2.5 & \tfrac{17}{6} & -\tfrac{1}{3} \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & \tfrac{23}{6} & \tfrac{1}{6} \\ \end{array} $$ Step 5: Prediction at chosen design point $x=2.5$ $$\begin{aligned} \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(2.5) &= \frac{5}{6} + 2.5 = \frac{5}{6} + \frac{15}{6} = \frac{20}{6} = \frac{10}{3} \approx 3.3 \end{aligned}$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Data xy0_hat <- data.frame( x_hat=c(1, 2, 3), y_hat=c(2, 2.5, 4)) ## Simple Linear Regression reg0 <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy0_hat) coef(reg0) ## (Intercept) x_hat ## 0.8333333 1.0000000 ## Sample Predictions predict(reg0) ## 1 2 3 ## 1.833333 2.833333 3.833333 resid(reg0) ## 1 2 3 ## 0.1666667 -0.3333333 0.1666667 ## Out-of-Sample predictions predict(reg0, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=c(2.5))) ## 1 ## 3.333333 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### **Simple Constant Regression** {-} Sometimes we restrict one coefficient of the simple linear model to zero, to get an even simpler model. Setting $b_{1}=0$ removes $\hat{x}_{i}$ from the model, so every observation gets the same fitted value. Our *simple constant model* is $$ \hat{y}_{i}=b_{0}+\hat{e}_{i}, $$ where the *coefficient* $b_{0}$ is a single number shared by every observation, and $\hat{y}_{i}$ is the data for observation $i$. The constant model is useful as a baseline: it is our best prediction of $\hat{y}_{i}$ when we ignore $\hat{x}_{i}$, and other regressions can be judged by how much they improve on it. For the constant model, the OLS problem is $$ \min_{b_{0}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_{i} - b_{0} \right)^2. $$ Setting the derivative to zero shows that the least-squares constant is the sample mean: $$\begin{aligned} \hat{b}_{0} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{y}_{i}}{n} = \hat{m}_{Y}. \end{aligned}$$ So every fitted value is the same, $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \hat{m}_{Y}$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Regress on a constant only: '~ 1' means an intercept and no slope reg_const <- lm(y_hat ~ 1, data=xy_hat) coef(reg_const) ## (Intercept) ## 7.788 # Same as the sample mean mean(xy_hat[, 'y_hat']) ## [1] 7.788 ``` ::: :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} **Regression Through the Origin** Setting $b_{0}=0$ instead forces the fitted line through the point $(0, 0)$. Our *simple model through the origin* is $$ \hat{y}_{i}=b_{1}\hat{x}_{i}+\hat{e}_{i}, $$ where the *coefficient* $b_{1}$ is a slope with no intercept. This model is useful when theory says $\hat{y}$ must be zero whenever $\hat{x}$ is zero, such as a firm's total cost when it has no fixed costs. Fit this model to the murder data, and compare its slope with the slope of the unrestricted line. Minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^{n} ( \hat{y}_{i} - b_{1}\hat{x}_{i} )^2$ gives $$\begin{aligned} \hat{b}_{1} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{x}_{i}\hat{y}_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{x}_{i}^{2}}. \end{aligned}$$ Unlike $\hat{c}_{XY}/\hat{v}_{X}$, this slope does not subtract the means $\hat{m}_{X}$ and $\hat{m}_{Y}$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Regress without an intercept: '0 +' drops b0 from the model reg_origin <- lm(y_hat ~ 0 + x_hat, data=xy_hat) coef(reg_origin) ## x_hat ## 0.1143623 # Manual verification sum(x_hat*y_hat)/sum(x_hat^2) ## [1] 0.1143623 # Scatter with the axes extended to the origin, then add all three fitted lines plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, xy_hat, col=grey(0, .5), pch=16, xlim=c(0, 100), ylim=c(0, max(y_hat)), main=NA, xlab='Population Share in Urban Area', ylab='Murder Arrests per 100K') abline(reg, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) abline(reg_origin, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2) abline(h=coef(reg_const), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lty=2) legend('topleft', legend=c('Unrestricted', 'Through origin', 'Constant'), col=c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), rgb(0, 0, 0, .8)), lwd=c(2, 1, 1), lty=c(1, 2, 2), bty='n') ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: No state is less than 32 percent urban, so the line is pinned to a point far from the data and its slope rises from about 0.02 to about 0.11. ::: ## Goodness of Fit After fitting the line, the next question is how much of the variation in $\hat{y}$ the line actually accounts for. :::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"} The *R-squared* (or *coefficient of determination*) $\hat{R}^{2}$ is the share of total variation in $\hat{y}_{i}$ that the model explains. Using the Total, Explained, and Residual sums of squares, $$\underbrace{\sum_{i}(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y})^2}_{\text{TSS}} = \underbrace{\sum_{i}(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}-\hat{m}_{Y})^2}_{\text{ESS}}+\underbrace{\sum_{i}\hat{e}_{i}^2}_{\text{RSS}},$$ $$\hat{R}^{2} = \frac{\hat{\text{ESS}}}{\hat{\text{TSS}}}=1-\frac{\hat{\text{RSS}}/n}{\hat{v}_{Y}},$$ where $\hat{v}_{Y}=\hat{\text{TSS}}/n$ is the variance of $\hat{y}$. Equivalently, $\hat{R}^{2}$ equals the squared Pearson correlation between the fitted values $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}$ and the actual $\hat{y}_{i}$; $\hat{r}_{YY^{\mathrm{fit}}}^{2}$. ::: $R^{2}$ always falls in $[0,1]$ and is useful as a single-number summary of how much of the variation in $\hat{y}$ the linear model accounts for. A value of $\hat{R}^{2}=1$ means perfect in-sample fit, and $\hat{R}^{2}=0$ means the model does no better than predicting the mean. The [simple constant regression](#simple-constant-regression) predicts the mean for every observation, so every term of its $\hat{\text{ESS}}$ is zero and its $\hat{R}^{2}=0$. The first qualitative check should still be a plot of the line over the data, however, since $R^{2}$ is only a summary. (Even a model with $\hat{R}^{2}$ near $1$ only describes how the mean of $\hat{y}$ differs across values of $\hat{x}$.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Manually Compute R2 e_hat <- resid(reg) RSS_n <- mean(e_hat^2) y_hat <- xy_hat[, 'y_hat'] v_hat <- mean((y_hat-mean(y_hat))^2) R2 <- 1 - RSS_n/v_hat R2 ## [1] 0.00484035 # Check R2 summary(reg)$r.squared ## [1] 0.00484035 # Double Check R2 R <- cor(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], predict(reg)) R^2 ## [1] 0.00484035 ``` ::: :::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"} We use the dataset $\{(1,2), (2,2.5), (3,4)\}$ to compute Goodness of fit. From before, we know that $\hat{m}_{Y} = \frac{17}{6}$ and the fitted values and residuals from the regression are $$\begin{gathered} \hat{y}_{1}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \frac{11}{6},\qquad \hat{y}_{2}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \frac{17}{6},\qquad \hat{y}_{3}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \frac{23}{6}.\\ \hat{e}_{1} = \frac{1}{6},\qquad \hat{e}_{2} = -\frac{1}{3},\qquad \hat{e}_{3} = \frac{1}{6}. \end{gathered}$$ Step 1. Total Sum of Squares (TSS) $$\begin{aligned} \hat{y}_{1} - \hat{m}_{Y} &= 2 - \frac{17}{6} = -\frac{5}{6}, \\ \hat{y}_{2} - \hat{m}_{Y} &= 2.5 - \frac{17}{6} = -\frac{1}{3}, \\ \hat{y}_{3} - \hat{m}_{Y} &= 4 - \frac{17}{6} = \frac{7}{6}. \end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\text{TSS}} &= \sum_{i} (\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y})^2 \\ &= \left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)^2 + \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{7}{6}\right)^2 \\ &= \frac{25}{36} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{49}{36} = \frac{78}{36} = \frac{13}{6}. \end{aligned}$$ Step 2. Explained Sum of Squares (ESS) $$ \hat{y}_{1}^{\mathrm{fit}} - \hat{m}_{Y} = -1,\qquad \hat{y}_{2}^{\mathrm{fit}} - \hat{m}_{Y} = 0,\qquad \hat{y}_{3}^{\mathrm{fit}} - \hat{m}_{Y} = 1. $$ $$ \hat{\text{ESS}} = \sum_{i} (\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} - \hat{m}_{Y})^2 = (-1)^2 + 0^2 + 1^2 = 2. $$ Step 3. Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) $$ \hat{\text{RSS}} = \sum_{i} \hat{e}_{i}^2 = \left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^2 + \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^2. $$ $$ \hat{\text{RSS}} = \frac{1}{36} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{36} = \frac{1}{36} + \frac{4}{36} + \frac{1}{36} = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}. $$ Step 4. Check the Decomposition $$ \hat{\text{ESS}} + \hat{\text{RSS}} = 2 + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{12}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{13}{6} = \hat{\text{TSS}}. $$ Step 5. Coefficient of Determination $$ \hat{R}^{2} = \frac{\hat{\text{ESS}}}{\hat{\text{TSS}}} = \frac{2}{13/6} = \frac{12}{13} \approx 0.92 $$ (Verification) $$ 1 - \frac{\hat{\text{RSS}}}{\hat{\text{TSS}}} = 1 - \frac{1/6}{13/6} = 1 - \frac{1}{13} = \frac{12}{13}. $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Compute R2 e0_hat <- resid(reg0) RSS0 <- sum(e0_hat^2) y0_hat <- xy0_hat[, 'y_hat'] TSS0 <- sum((y0_hat-mean(y0_hat))^2) R2_0 <- 1 - RSS0/TSS0 R2_0 ## [1] 0.9230769 # compare with our calculation: 12/13 12/13 ## [1] 0.9230769 # compare with our intuitive benchmark: squared correlation of actuals and fitted values cor(y0_hat, predict(reg0))^2 ## [1] 0.9230769 ``` ::: ::: #### **Cross-Validation** {-} To measure out-of-sample fit and predictive power, we average the squared errors of predictions for held-out observations [@Allen1974; @Stone1974; @HallRacine2015]. :::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"} The *leave-one-out cross-validation* error measures how well a model predicts observations that were not used to fit it, $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\text{CV}} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i}) \right]^2, \end{aligned}$$ where $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i})$ is the model's prediction at $\hat{x}_{i}$ from a fit that excluded observation $i$. ::: $\hat{\text{CV}}$ is useful for comparing models by how well they predict new observations, rather than the observations used to fit them. It drops one observation at a time, like the [jackknife](01_05_Sampling.qmd#jackknife-distribution). A model that fits the noise in the sample predicts held-out observations poorly, so its $\hat{\text{CV}}$ rises above its in-sample average $\hat{\text{RSS}}/n$. The *out-of-sample R-squared* replaces the fitted values in $\hat{R}^{2}=1-(\hat{\text{RSS}}/n)/\hat{v}_{Y}$ with the held-out predictions $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i})$. The average squared residual $\hat{\text{RSS}}/n$ then becomes $\hat{\text{CV}}$, and the variance $\hat{v}_{Y}$ becomes its leave-one-out version $\hat{v}_{Y}^{\text{CV}}$, which gives $$\begin{aligned} \hat{R}^{2}_{\text{CV}} &= 1 - \frac{\hat{\text{CV}}}{\hat{v}_{Y}^{\text{CV}}}, \\ \hat{v}_{Y}^{\text{CV}} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}^{(-i)} \right]^2, \end{aligned}$$ where $\hat{m}_{Y}^{(-i)}$ is the mean of $\hat{y}$ without observation $i$. Since $\hat{v}_{Y}^{\text{CV}}$ is the $\hat{\text{CV}}$ of the [simple constant regression](#simple-constant-regression), that model has $\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{CV}}=0$. Unlike $\hat{R}^{2}$, $\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{CV}}$ can be negative and is when a model predicts held-out observations worse than the mean of the other observations would. Unlike $\hat{R}^{2}$, the out-of-sample version is not equivalent to the squared correlation between the observations and the predictions ($\hat{y}_{i}$ and $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i})$). The code below refits the line $n$ times, each time without one state, and predicts that state's murder arrest rate. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Leave-one-out errors for the line and for the mean n <- nrow(xy_hat) loo_errors <- rep(NA, n) loo_errors_mean <- rep(NA, n) for(i in seq_len(n)){ xy_i <- xy_hat[-i, ] # drop state i reg_i <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_i) # Predict state i from the fit without state i y_pred_i <- predict(reg_i, newdata=xy_hat[i, ]) loo_errors[i] <- xy_hat[i, 'y_hat'] - y_pred_i # Compare state i with the mean of the other states loo_errors_mean[i] <- xy_hat[i, 'y_hat'] - mean(xy_i[, 'y_hat']) } # CV cv_hat <- mean(loo_errors^2) cv_hat ## [1] 20.13806 # Leave-one-out version of the variance v_cv_hat <- mean(loo_errors_mean^2) v_cv_hat ## [1] 19.35762 # Out-of-sample R-squared r2_cv <- 1 - cv_hat/v_cv_hat # Correlation of the observations and the held-out predictions, then its square r_cv <- cor(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'] - loo_errors) r2_gen_cv <- r_cv^2 c(R2=R2, R2_CV=r2_cv, r_CV=r_cv, R2_gen_CV=r2_gen_cv) ## R2 R2_CV r_CV R2_gen_CV ## 0.00484035 -0.04031697 -0.46825489 0.21926264 ``` ::: The line predicts held-out states worse than the states it was fit to: its $\hat{\text{CV}}$ of about $20.1$ is above its $\hat{\text{RSS}}/n$ of about $18.5$. Its $\hat{\text{CV}}$ is also above $\hat{v}_{Y}^{\text{CV}}$ of about $19.4$, so its $\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{CV}}$ of about $-0.04$ is negative: out of sample, the line predicts murder arrests worse than the mean of the other states would. Its squared correlation of about $0.22$ looks better than its $\hat{R}^{2}$ of about $0.005$, but only because squaring hides the sign of the correlation, which is about $-0.47$. Dropping a state with a high murder arrest rate lowers the prediction for that state, so the held-out predictions tend to move against the observations. :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} We can also compare the line with the [simple constant regression](#simple-constant-regression) out of sample. The code below repeats the loop for the constant model, whose held-out prediction for each state is the mean of the other states. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Leave-one-out prediction errors for the constant model loo_errors_const <- rep(NA, n) for(i in seq_len(n)){ xy_i <- xy_hat[-i, ] # drop state i reg_const_i <- lm(y_hat ~ 1, data=xy_i) # Predict state i from the fit without state i y_pred_i <- predict(reg_const_i, newdata=xy_hat[i, ]) loo_errors_const[i] <- xy_hat[i, 'y_hat'] - y_pred_i } cv_const_hat <- mean(loo_errors_const^2) r2_cv_const <- 1 - cv_const_hat/v_cv_hat # In-sample and out-of-sample fit of both models fit_compare <- rbind( Line=c(RSS_n=RSS_n, CV=cv_hat, R2=R2, R2_CV=r2_cv), Constant=c(RSS_n=sum(resid(reg_const)^2)/n, CV=cv_const_hat, R2=summary(reg_const)$r.squared, R2_CV=r2_cv_const)) round(fit_compare, 3) ## RSS_n CV R2 R2_CV ## Line 18.501 20.138 0.005 -0.04 ## Constant 18.591 19.358 0.000 0.00 ``` ::: In sample, the line fits slightly better than the constant model, as it must, since the constant model is the line with $b_{1}=0$. Out of sample, the order flips: the line's $\hat{\text{CV}}$ is about $20.1$, while the constant model's is about $19.4$. Urbanization explains so little of the variation in murder arrests that estimating a slope adds more noise to the predictions than it removes. The constant model's $\hat{\text{CV}}$ is exactly $\hat{v}_{Y}^{\text{CV}}$, so its $\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{CV}}$ is $0$, the same as its in-sample $\hat{R}^{2}$. With $\hat{v}_{Y}$ in the denominator instead, even the constant model would score below $0$, because each held-out prediction is the mean of the other $49$ states, while $\hat{m}_{Y}$ also includes the state being predicted. ::: ## Variability Estimates A regression coefficient is a statistic, so it has its own sampling distribution that we want to summarize. As in [Standard Errors](01_05_Sampling.qmd#standard-errors), we summarize that spread with the *standard error*: the standard deviation of the statistic's sampling distribution. There, we computed bootstrap standard errors for the mean and the median of one variable. The slope works the same way, except that we resample whole rows of the data, so each $\hat{x}_{i}$ stays paired with its $\hat{y}_{i}$. For the slope, the standard error describes how much $\hat{b}_{1}$ would change if we drew another sample of $n$ observations. We write $\text{SE}(B_{1})$ for the theoretical standard error of the slope estimator $B_{1}$, and $\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{1})$ for its estimate computed from the observed sample. The standard error is distinct from the *standard deviation* of $\hat{y}$, which measures variability of observations *within* a single sample. From a standard error, we can build a *confidence interval*: a range of values consistent with our data at a chosen level. Note that values reported by your computer do not necessarily satisfy this definition. To estimate variability, we will use the data-driven methods from [Resampling Intervals](01_07_Intervals.qmd#resampling-intervals). (For some theoretical background, see also .) #### **Bootstrap** {-} There are several resampling techniques. One main one is the bootstrap, which resamples with replacement for an arbitrary number of iterations. When bootstrapping a dataset with $n$ observations, you randomly resample all $n$ rows in your data set $B$ times. We can then just take the percentiles of the bootstrap distribution. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Original OLS coefficient slope <- coef(reg)[2] # Number of observations n <- nrow(xy_hat) # Bootstrap Sampling Distribution boot_coefs <- rep(NA, 399) for(i in seq_along(boot_coefs)){ b_id <- sample(n, replace=TRUE) xy_boot <- xy_hat[b_id, ] reg_b <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_boot) slope_b <- coef(reg_b)[2] boot_coefs[i] <- slope_b } # Plot Bootstrap Sampling Distribution # + Percentile CI hist(boot_coefs, breaks=25, main=NA, border=NA, freq=FALSE, xlab=expression(hat(b)[1])) title('Bootstrap Distribution with 95% CIs', font.main=1) boot_ci_percentile <- quantile(boot_coefs, probs=c(.025, .975)) abline(v=boot_ci_percentile, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### **Normal Approximation with Jackknife SE** {-} We also use the jackknife, which loops through each row of the dataset. In each iteration of the loop, we drop that observation from the dataset and reestimate the statistic of interest. We then calculate the standard deviation of the statistic across all subsamples to get jackknife standard errors and, assuming the data are approximately normal, use Normal quantiles to construct a CI.^[Recall that jackknife standard errors need to be rescaled because each jackknife resample is too similar to the next. For this reason, we also do not simply take the percentiles of the jackknife distribution. We can also calculate the standard deviation of the statistic across all bootstrap samples instead.] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Jackknife Sampling Distribution for OLS Coefficient jack_coefs <- rep(NA, n) for(i in seq_along(jack_coefs)){ xy_i <- xy_hat[-i, ] reg_i <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_i) slope_i <- coef(reg_i)[2] jack_coefs[i] <- slope_i } jack_se <- sqrt((n - 1)/n * sum((jack_coefs - mean(jack_coefs))^2)) # Plot Estimated Sampling Distribution # Grid spans four jackknife SEs on either side of the estimate x <- seq(slope - 4*jack_se, slope + 4*jack_se, length.out=500) fx <- dnorm(x, mean(jack_coefs), jack_se) plot(x, fx, type='l', bty='n', col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), xlab=expression(hat(b)[1])) title('Normal Approx. with 95% CIs', font.main=1) # Normal Approx Confidence Interval jack_ci_normal <- qnorm(c(.025, .975), slope, jack_se) abline(v=jack_ci_normal, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=2) # Bootstrap Quantiles abline(v=boot_ci_percentile, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) legend('topright', lty=c(1, 2), lwd=2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), bty='n', cex=.75, title='Confidence Interval', legend=c('Bootstrap Percentile', 'Normal Approx.')) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: In any case, a $95\%$ confidence interval should contain the population slope in about $95\%$ of samples. Any one sample can miss it by a fair amount. ## Hypothesis Tests We can also use resampling to test a null hypothesis, most often of "no relationship". We are rarely interested in computing standard errors and conducting hypothesis tests for simple linear regressions in practice, but work through the ideas with two variables before moving to analyze multiple variables. #### **Invert a CI** {-} One main way to conduct hypothesis tests is to examine whether a confidence interval contains a hypothesized value. Does the slope coefficient equal $0$? We already have a bootstrap percentile interval for $\hat{b}_{1}$, so we check whether it contains $0$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Bootstrap distribution of the slope from above, with zero added to the plot hist(boot_coefs, breaks=25, main=NA, border=NA, freq=FALSE, xlab=expression(hat(b)[1]), xlim=range(c(0, boot_coefs))) title('Bootstrap Distribution with 95% CI', font.main=1) abline(v=boot_ci_percentile, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) abline(v=0, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Does the 95% interval contain zero? boot_ci_percentile ## 2.5% 97.5% ## -0.08014891 0.10154965 unname(boot_ci_percentile[1] <= 0 & boot_ci_percentile[2] >= 0) ## [1] TRUE ``` ::: The interval contains $0$, so a slope of zero is consistent with the data at the $95\%$ level. #### **Impose the Null**{-} We can also compute a null distribution. We focus on the simplest: simulations that each impose the null hypothesis and re-estimate the statistic of interest. Specifically, we compute the distribution of slopes on data with randomly reshuffled outcomes (imposing the null), and compare how extreme the observed slope is. We can sample with replacement (i.e., the null bootstrap) or without (permutation), just as with the [correlation](02_14_Associations.qmd#cardinal-data) statistic. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Null Distribution for Reg Coef null_coefs <- rep(NA, 399) for(b in seq_along(null_coefs)){ # Permuted data xy_perm <- xy_hat xy_perm[, 'y_hat'] <- sample( xy_perm[, 'y_hat'], replace=FALSE) #Bootstrap: replace=T # Redo regression reg_b <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_perm) null_coefs[b] <- coef(reg_b)[2] } # Null Distribution hist(null_coefs, breaks=25, main=NA, border=NA, freq=FALSE, xlab=expression(hat(b)[1]), xlim=range(null_coefs, slope)) title('Null Distribution', font.main=1) # Middle 95% of the permuted slopes null_ci <- quantile(null_coefs, probs=c(.025, .975)) abline(v=null_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) # Observed value abline(v=slope, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Permutations are common when testing against "no association". From permuted data, we can calculate a *$p$-value*: the probability you would see something at least as extreme as your statistic under the null (assuming your null hypothesis was true, see [$p$-values](01_08_HypothesisTests.qmd#p-values)). We calculate the $p$-value directly from the null distribution. Smaller $p$-values suggest more evidence against the null. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Two Sided Test for P(|b1| >= |observed b1| | Null of b1=0) F_hat <- ecdf(abs(null_coefs)) p_slope <- 1-F_hat(abs(slope)) p_slope ## [1] 0.6190476 plot(F_hat, xlim=range(abs(null_coefs), abs(slope)), xlab=expression( abs(hat(b)[1]) ), main=NA) title('Null Distribution', font.main=1) abline(v=abs(slope), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Interpret the $p$-value computed above. It is the fraction of the null distribution at least as extreme as the observed $\hat{b}_{1}$. Suppose the code returned $p=0.02$: in a world where the slope is truly zero, only $2\%$ of samples would produce a $|\hat{b}_{1}|$ this large, so under the common $5\%$ rule ($0.02 < 0.05$) we reject the null of no relationship. A larger value such as $p=0.30$ would mean such a $\hat{b}_{1}$ is unremarkable under the null, so we would fail to reject. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Hard decision rule at the 5% level if(p_slope < 0.05){ 'reject the null of no relationship' } else { 'fail to reject the null of no relationship' } ## [1] "fail to reject the null of no relationship" ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"} Suppose you have data on years of schooling and hourly wages for all $3294$ workers in `Wages1`. Conduct a linear regression. Summarize the model relationship and how well it fits the data. Then construct a $95\%$ bootstrap confidence interval for the slope coefficient. Finally, compute a permutation $p$-value for the null hypothesis of no relationship between schooling and wages. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data(Wages1, package='Ecdat') xy2_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')] colnames(xy2_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage # Regression and goodness of fit reg2 <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_hat) coef(reg2) ## (Intercept) x_hat ## -0.7225066 0.5571617 summary(reg2)$r.squared ## [1] 0.07980201 # Bootstrap percentile CI for the slope slope2 <- coef(reg2)[2] boot_coefs2 <- rep(NA, 399) for(b in seq_along(boot_coefs2)){ b_id <- sample(nrow(xy2_hat), replace=TRUE) xy2_boot <- xy2_hat[b_id, ] reg2_b <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_boot) boot_coefs2[b] <- coef(reg2_b)[2] } quantile(boot_coefs2, probs=c(.025, .975)) ## 2.5% 97.5% ## 0.4946767 0.6284096 # Permutation p-value, using the slope as the statistic null_coefs2 <- rep(NA, 399) for(b in seq_along(null_coefs2)){ xy2_perm <- xy2_hat xy2_perm[, 'y_hat'] <- sample(xy2_perm[, 'y_hat'], replace=FALSE) reg2_b <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_perm) null_coefs2[b] <- coef(reg2_b)[2] } # Middle 95% of the permuted slopes quantile(null_coefs2, probs=c(.025, .975)) ## 2.5% 97.5% ## -0.06491886 0.06591674 F2_hat <- ecdf(abs(null_coefs2)) 1-F2_hat(abs(slope2)) ## [1] 0 ``` ::: Each extra year of schooling goes with a higher hourly wage, on average. The $\hat{R}^{2}$ is small, so schooling alone leaves most of the variation in wages unexplained. The bootstrap interval is far from zero. The observed slope of about $0.56$ is also far outside the middle $95\%$ of permuted slopes, from about $-0.06$ to $0.07$, so the $p$-value is essentially zero. ::: #### **Caveats**{-} We could also use hard decision rules, such as "$p < 0.05$ is a statistically significant finding". However, just like confidence intervals, those hard decision rules can be sensitive to somewhat arbitrary choices (Why a bootstrap percentile interval instead of a jackknife Normal one? Why test at the $95\%$ level rather than $90\%$?) "No association" is the [most common null hypothesis](01_08_HypothesisTests.qmd#choosing-a-null) in practice, but we can also use bootstrapping to test against other specific hypothesized values of $\beta_{1}$, the population slope. The simplest way is to check whether $\beta_{1}$ lies inside the bootstrap interval for $\hat{b}_{1}$. To impose the null instead, you recenter the bootstrap distribution of $\hat{b}_{1}$ around the hypothetical value, as we did for the mean in [Impose the Null](01_08_HypothesisTests.qmd#impose-the-null). In the known-population check above, the population slope is `population_slope`, which we could compute only because we pretended `Wages1` was the whole population. Although two-sided hypothesis tests are most common, you can also test one-sided hypotheses. #### **Standardized Slopes**{-} Software typically reports a *$t$-value* for each coefficient, which divides the coefficient by its standard error: $\hat{t} = \frac{\hat{b}_{1}}{\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{1})}$, where $\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{1})$ is the estimated standard error of the coefficient. For reasons we won't go into in this class, $\hat{t}$ is often used instead of $\hat{b}_{1}$ as the test statistic. As a final example, we redo the permutation test with $\hat{t}$, using the jackknife standard error from above. Each permutation recomputes both the slope and its jackknife standard error. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create t-stat with jackknife SE t_hat <- slope/jack_se # Null Distribution for t-stat null_t <- rep(NA, 399) for(b in seq_along(null_t)){ # Permuted data xy_perm <- xy_hat xy_perm[, 'y_hat'] <- sample( xy_perm[, 'y_hat'], replace=FALSE) # Redo regression reg_b <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_perm) slope_b <- coef(reg_b)[2] # Redo Jackknife SEs jack_coefs_b <- rep(NA, nrow(xy_perm)) for(i in seq_along(jack_coefs_b)){ xy_perm_i <- xy_perm[-i, ] reg_b_i <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_perm_i) jack_coefs_b[i] <- coef(reg_b_i)[2] } n_b <- length(jack_coefs_b) jack_se_b <- sqrt((n_b - 1)/n_b * sum((jack_coefs_b - mean(jack_coefs_b))^2)) # Redo t with Jackknife SE null_t[b] <- slope_b/jack_se_b } # Null Distribution hist(null_t, breaks=25, main=NA, border=NA, freq=FALSE, xlab=expression(hat(t)), xlim=range(null_t, t_hat)) title('Null Distribution of t', font.main=1) abline(v=quantile(null_t, probs=c(.025, .975)), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) abline(v=t_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Two Sided Test for P(|t| >= |observed t| | Null of t=0), next to the slope version F_t_hat <- ecdf(abs(null_t)) p_t <- 1-F_t_hat(abs(t_hat)) c(slope=p_slope, t=p_t) ## slope t ## 0.6190476 0.6791980 ``` ::: Both $p$-values are large, so both tests fail to reject the null of no relationship between urbanization and murder arrests. ## Regression and Causation The same caveats about "correlation is not causation" from [Association is not Causation](02_14_Associations.qmd#association-is-not-causation) extend to regression. You may be tempted to use the term "the effect", but that interpretation of a regression coefficient assumes the linear model is true. If you fit a line to a non-linear relationship, then you will still get back a coefficient even though there is no singular *the* effect: the true relationship is non-linear! Also consider a classic example, *Anscombe's Quartet* [@Anscombe1973], which shows four very different datasets that give the same linear regression coefficient. Notice that you understand the problem because we used scatterplots to visualize the data.^[The same principle holds when comparing two groups: ] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Anscombe's Quartet par(mfrow=c(2, 2)) for(i in 1:4){ x_hat <- anscombe[, paste0('x', i)] y_hat <- anscombe[, paste0('y', i)] plot(x_hat, y_hat, ylim=c(4, 13), xlim=c(4, 20), pch=16, col=grey(0, .6), main=NA, xlab=paste0('x', i), ylab=paste0('y', i)) reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat) b <- round(coef(reg)[2], 2) p <- round(summary(reg)$coefficients[2, 4], 4) abline(reg, col=rgb(1, 0.6, 0, .8)) title(paste0('Slope=', b, ', p=', p), font.main=1) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_15_SimpleRegression_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## For an even better example, see `Datasaurus Dozen' #browseURL( #'https://bookdown.org/paul/applied-data-visualization/ #why-look-the-datasaurus-dozen.html') ``` ::: It is true that linear regression "is the best linear predictor of the nonlinear regression function if the mean-squared error is used as the loss function" [@camerontrivedi2005, p. 92]. But this is not a carte-blanche justification for OLS, as the best of the bad predictors is still a bad predictor. For many economic applications, it is more helpful to think and speak of "dose response curves" instead of "the effect". While adding interaction terms or squared terms allows one to incorporate heterogeneity and non-linearity, they change several features of the model (most of which are not intended). Often, there are nonsensical predicted values. For example, if most of your age data are between $[23,65]$, a quadratic term can imply silly things for people aged $10$ or $90$. Nonetheless, linear regression provides an important piece of quantitative information that is understood by many. All models are an approximation, and sometimes only unimportant nuances are missing from a vanilla linear model. Other times, that model can be seriously misleading. (This is especially true if you are making policy recommendations based on a universal "the effect".) As an exploratory tool, linear regression is a good guess but one whose point estimates should not be taken too seriously (in which case, the standard errors are also much less important). Before trying to find a regression specification that makes sense for the entire dataset, explore local relationships. ## Exercises 1. We measured its goodness of fit with $\hat{R}^{2}$ in sample and with leave-one-out cross-validation out of sample. For the murder data, the line predicted held-out states worse than the constant model, and its $\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{CV}}$ was about $-0.04$. We built confidence intervals and $p$-values by resampling the data with the bootstrap, the jackknife, and permutations. The correlation examples showed both causation without linear correlation and correlation without causation. The three-observation worked example $\{(1,2),(2,2.5),(3,4)\}$ traced through every step by hand and produced slope $\hat{b}_{1}=1$, intercept $\hat{b}_{0}=5/6$, $\hat{\text{TSS}}=13/6$, $\hat{\text{RSS}}=1/6$, and $\hat{R}^{2}=12/13\approx 0.92$.
